articles.title: I Had 5,000 Screenshots and Couldn’t Find Any, So I Built: SnapRecall-Type What You Remember, Find the Screenshot
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built SnapRecall is a screenshot search tool. It watches your screenshots folder, lets an AI model read every image in the background, and builds a private search index. Later, you type whatever you remember about the screenshot ("rahul payment 2500", "docker permission error", "wo flight ticket wala") and the matching screenshots show up. How I got the idea I take a lot of screenshots. A payment confirmation, a WhatsApp chat I might need as proof, an error message I want to Google later, a ticket, a recipe, a random detail from a group chat. I never organize them, because the whole point of a screenshot is that it takes one second. The cost shows up later. My screenshots folder has thousands of files, all named like this: screenshot_2026-10-24-14-55-16.png screenshot_2026-10-24-14-55-41.png screenshot_2026-10-24-15-02-07.png When I need one specific image, those names tell me nothing. I end up scrolling through hundreds of nearly identical thumbnails, squinting at each one, and sometimes giving up. It is not a big problem, but it happens often, and it is exactly the kind of tedious work that a computer should do instead of me. When I read the "slow and steady" theme, this was the first thing I thought of. It is a task that should happen quietly in the background, with no effort from me, while I do something else. Two ideas, one choice I had two possible solutions: Rename on save. The moment a screenshot is taken, an AI reads it, summarizes it, and renames the file with the important words. A WhatsApp chat about rent becomes something like whatsapp_rahul_rent_payment.png. Search by memory. Leave the files alone. When I cannot find a screenshot, I type the words I remember from inside it, and the app shows me the matches. Renaming looked simple, but when I thought it through, it had problems. A filename is one guess about what I will remember later, and the AI's guess is often not the thing I remember. A screenshot of a chat could be filed under the contact's name, the topic, or the amount, and I might search by any of them. Renaming files can also break references in other apps or sync tools, and after a few thousand files, long auto-generated names start to look the same again. Search works with whatever I happen to remember, and it does not touch my files. So I chose search as the core, and I treat smart renaming as a possible add-on for later (with a preview and an undo, not silent changes). Who it is for Anyone with a messy screenshots folder: students who screenshot notes, developers who save error messages, and people who screenshot payments, chats and tickets as proof. I also built it with Hindi and Hinglish in mind, because that is how I actually think and type. A lot of the text in my screenshots is in Hindi or mixed, and I did not want a tool that only works for clean English. Features Background indexing: new screenshots are picked up automatically soon after they are saved A slow, throttled backfill of your old screenshots, so a big backlog never needs your attention A vision model reads each screenshot and produces a short summary, tags, an app type (chat, payment, code, error, ticket...) and the text it can see Hybrid search: keyword matching for exact names, amounts and error codes, plus semantic search for vague memories English, Hindi and Hinglish queries A simple React interface with a thumbnail grid, a larger preview, and live indexing progress with pause and resume Demo Code GitHub repo How I Built It The stack Backend: Python and FastAPI Frontend: React (Vite, TypeScript) Storage: SQLite for everything, with FTS5 for keyword search and sqlite-vec for vectors Folder watching: watchdog Models: Gemma for reading screenshots, plus an embedding model for semantic search I chose SQLite on purpose. For a personal tool, one file with no server to run is a big advantage, and it keeps the whole thing light on a laptop. The pipeline Screenshots folder | v Watcher + folder scanner -> job queue (SQLite) one image at a time, with a pause downscale image -> Gemma: summary, tags, app type, visible text embed the combined text SQLite: metadata + keyword index + vector index ^ React UI -> FastAPI -> hybrid search (keyword + semantic, merged) For each screenshot, the worker downscales the image (so it does not send more pixels than needed), asks Gemma for a short summary, a few tags, the type of screenshot, and the important text it can read, then turns that combined text into an embedding. Everything is stored in SQLite next to the original file path. Why the search is hybrid I tried to think about how I actually look for screenshots, and I realized there are two very different cases. Sometimes I remember something exact: a name, an amount like "2500", an error code. Keyword search is best for this, because semantic search can blur exact tokens together. Other times my memory is vague: "that screenshot of the bus ticket" or "the chat where we decided the date". Here, keyword search fails if the exact words do not match, but semantic search can still find it because it matches meaning. So SnapRecall runs both searches and merges the two ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which rewards results that rank well in either list without needing to compare their scores directly. It is a simple technique, and it covers both ways I search. Slow and steady, on purpose This is where the theme became a design rule instead of a slogan. Reading thousands of images with a model is heavy work. If a tool tries to do it all at once, it either freezes your computer or burns through your API limits and fails halfway. So the indexer is built to be patient: It processes one image at a time, with a configurable pause between images It backs off and retries when the API rate-limits it, instead of treating that as a failure It can pause itself when a daily request budget is reached, and it can be paused and resumed from the interface If the app is closed or crashes, it picks up where it stopped when it starts again You can keep working while it runs. It is the opposite of a tool that demands your attention. Local first, then hosted, and why I changed My original plan was fully local: Gemma through Ollama, Tesseract for OCR, everything on my own machine. Then I looked at my laptop. It is old and weak, and running a vision model on it would be painfully slow, if it ran at all. So for this submission I changed course and used Gemma 4 through the Gemini API. The backend does not become heavy this way: it only watches a folder, stores data in SQLite and serves a few endpoints, so my laptop handles it fine, and the heavy model work happens remotely. I also turned off the OCR step in hosted mode, because Gemma already returns the text it sees. I built the model layer behind a provider switch, so the same pipeline can point to a hosted API or to a local Ollama server. That was partly a practical decision and partly a way to keep the project honest about the open vs hosted tradeoff, which I explain below. One thing to be clear about: in hosted mode, the embeddings come from a hosted embedding model that is not open-source, so that part of the stack is not open. I also used an AI assistant to help plan the architecture and write parts of the code. I am still testing how well it all works together, which brings me to the status at the end of this post. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? The prompt asks some direct questions, so I will answer them directly, including the places where my answer is "not yet" or "not really". Does running your own model mean it works without internet? In principle, yes, and that is one of the main reasons I picked an open model family. In the mode I used for this submission, no: I ran Gemma through a hosted API, so it needs an internet connection. The project is designed so that a local Ollama setup should work offline once the models are downloaded, but I have not been able to test that on my own hardware, so I will not claim it works. Does it keep personal messages and files on your own machine? This is the point that matters most for this particular project. Screenshots are one of the most private things on a phone or laptop: OTPs, bank messages, personal chats, ID photos. Uploading thousands of them to a third party is a real cost, and many people would rightly refuse. In hosted mode, my screenshots do go to the model provider, so please do not treat that mode as private. What open weights give me is a private option. The same model family can run on a machine the user controls, and a user who cares about privacy can choose that path. With a closed vision API, there would be no such option: the only way to use it is to send the images out. Does it let you set it up once and never pay again? With a local model, that is the idea: after the setup, indexing 10,000 screenshots costs only electricity. With the hosted route I used, I am on a free tier with limits, and those limits shaped the design directly. The worker is throttled, it respects rate limits, and it has a daily request budget, because indexing a big backlog through a hosted API would otherwise hit those limits fast. A closed API charged per image would add a cost on every re-index, which matters a lot for a tool whose job is to process thousands of images. Where did the open approach work better than a closed one? The honest answer is flexibility, not raw quality. Because Gemma's weights are open, the same model was available to me as a hosted API when my laptop could not run it, and it is available to someone with a stronger machine to run privately. I could pick the deployment that matched my hardware, and I can change that choice later without rewriting the project. Prize Categories Best Use of Gemma: Gemma is the model that actually reads the screenshots. Its summary, tags, app type and visible text are what the whole search index is built from, so without it the project does not work. I used Gemma 4 through the Gemini API. Where This Stands This is an idea I took from a real annoyance to a working design in a short time, and it still needs testing. Thank you for taking the time to read this.

articles.title: Week 3's DEV challenge
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady Lazy Meal Diary: an offline cooking helper for students, on my phone My PC is still broken. Last week's post was about the day it died, and it's still not fixed, so this build also had to run on the only computer I have left: my Redmi 13. The problem Student cooking has the same loop every week. You cook something decent on Tuesday, forget it by Friday, and stand in front of the same few ingredients with no idea what to make. I wanted a diary I could talk to in one line, one that remembers what I cooked and suggests something similar later. What I built App: PocketPal AI (open-source), running fully on the phone Model: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (q4_k_m, about 1.1 GB), an open-weight model A system prompt that makes it a meal diary for a Nigerian student with one burner and a small budget One dedicated chat for the whole week How the "memory" works The model has no memory of its own. PocketPal keeps the chat, and the model re-reads the whole chat every time I send a message. So as long as I keep one chat open, Tuesday's meal is still in front of it on Friday. Why open matters here It works offline, so no data is spent. My eating habits and budget stay on my phone and not on someone else's server. It costs nothing per message, so I never pay for it. I can change the model, the prompt, and the generation settings. What worked I logged "Tuesday: egg and indomie with tomato" and "Wednesday: beans and garri". On Friday I asked for something similar to Tuesday's meal, and the model correctly named "egg and indomie with tomato". Replies came in about 2 seconds after the model loaded, at around 6 tokens per second. What didn't A repetition loop. My first attempt made the model write a random recipe and then repeat "1/4 cup chopped cilantro" over and over. I fixed it by lowering temperature, raising the repeat penalty, and capping the reply length. It ignored my "one short line" rule. When I logged a meal, it often answered with a recipe instead of a short confirmation. It ignored my new ingredients. On Friday I said I had eggs, rice, and pepper. It recalled Tuesday's meal but used none of those ingredients, and it invented "egg noodles". A 1.5B model on a phone can recall what's in the chat, but it doesn't follow detailed instructions well. Honest note This is a prompt-driven tool, not a trained model, and a long chat could overload a small model's context. I tested four messages in one chat and not with another student. Next I'd try a 3B model, store meals in a small file so memory doesn't depend on chat length, and test it with a real classmate. Once my PC is fixed, I'd like to turn this into a proper build with a bigger model and a saved meal log, so the memory doesn't depend on a chat staying short. Screenshots (Attach: the cilantro loop, the Tuesday entry reply, and the Friday reply.)

articles.title: LazyMorning — Your Overnight Life Assistant
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady What I Built Mornings are often ruined by a barrage of questions: What was I working on yesterday? Which deadlines are due today? What do I need to tackle first? This morning decision fatigue drains our best mental energy before the day even begins. LazyMorning is an overnight personal life assistant designed to let you wake up with complete clarity and zero panic. While you sleep, LazyMorning analyzes your active tasks, captured notes, upcoming deadlines, and approved documents to prepare a serene, focused Morning Briefing delivered right as you start your day. What it does: Today's Focus: Synthesizes a calming, single-sentence priority focus for the morning. Top 3 Priorities: Extracts the three highest-impact tasks with explicit reasoning and urgency tags. Upcoming Deadlines: Clear timeline of impending deliverables so nothing slips through the cracks. Unfinished Items: Quick tally of pending items requiring future attention. Suggested First Step: Gives you an immediate, low-friction, concrete first action (e.g. "Spend 10 minutes reviewing the first slide") to kick off your day with calm momentum instead of paralysis. Who gets to be a little lazier because of it? Developers, students, founders, and busy professionals who want to reclaim peaceful mornings. Instead of spending 30 minutes every morning triaging sticky notes, Slack messages, and todo lists, you open your LazyMorning dashboard, sip your coffee with our relaxed sloth mascot, and know exactly what to do next. Demo 🌐 Live Deployed App: https://lazymorning.onrender.com/ 📖 Interactive API Documentation (Swagger): https://lazymorning.onrender.com/docs Code Check out the full open-source repository on GitHub: 👉 https://github.com/abhinavnayak21/LazyMorning-x-MLH abhinavnayak21 / LazyMorning-x-MLH 🦥 LazyMorning — Your Overnight Life Assistant "Slow plans, brighter days." Built for the "Slow and Steady" Open-Source AI Challenge. LazyMorning is a privacy-first, 100% local personal morning assistant. While you sleep, LazyMorning reviews your active tasks, notes, deadlines, and approved files to prepare a serene, focused morning briefing—eliminating morning decision fatigue and friction. 📸 Design & Experience Crafted to match modern, calming aesthetics with an adorable mascot and clean cards: Dashboard: Daily greeting, Today's Focus hero banner, 4 vital metrics (Top Priorities, Upcoming Deadlines, Pending Tasks, Total Notes), latest briefing summary, and quick actions. Morning Briefing: Today's Focus, Top 3 Priorities (with reasoning and deadlines), Upcoming Deadlines list, Unfinished Items, and a gentle Suggested First Step. Notes: Create, organize, tag, and search thoughts and ideas. Tasks: Track priorities (High, Medium, Low), due dates, and instant checkbox completion. Imported Files: Scan and import local .txt… View on GitHub How I Built It LazyMorning is designed from the ground up around open-source AI and private local-first computing: 1. Open-Source AI Architecture Model: Qwen 2.5 (7B Instruct) — a state-of-the-art open-weight model renowned for structured reasoning, nuance, and concise summarization. Hybrid Inference Pipeline: Local Ollama: Runs 100% locally on personal machines via Ollama (qwen2.5:7b). Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared): Allows remote deployment on Render to securely reach local Ollama instances over an encrypted Cloudflare Tunnel without public port forwarding. Cloudflare Workers AI: Cloudflare’s serverless GPU edge option running @cf/qwen/qwen2.5-7b-instruct for 24/7 cloud availability. Zero-Crash Local Fallback Engine: If Ollama or the network is ever unreachable, an intelligent rule-based synthesizer steps in automatically, ensuring you never miss a briefing. Hallucination Validator: AI outputs are strictly cross-referenced against the SQLite database to ensure the model never invents ghost tasks or fake deadlines. 2. Tech Stack Frontend: Streamlit styled with custom modern CSS and base64 vector art to create a warm, calming aesthetic with our sloth mascot. Backend: FastAPI with async REST routing and OpenAPI documentation. Database: SQLite with SQLAlchemy ORM for lightweight, durable local persistence. Overnight Scheduler: APScheduler running in-process for automated morning digest generation at configurable local wake-up times. Automated Tests: Comprehensive Pytest suite covering CRUD operations, file security gates, AI fallback, and hallucination filters (100% pass rate). 3. Privacy & File Approval Gate To prevent accidental data leakage, imported local .txt and .md files enter a pending state. Only files explicitly toggled to "✅ Approved for AI" are included in the morning briefing context. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Your daily notes, personal reflections, project roadmaps, and client meeting takeaways are sensitive personal data. Sending them to closed, proprietary cloud AI APIs: Risks privacy: Exposes private thoughts and proprietary work to third-party data collection and training pipelines. Introduces toll booths: Closed APIs charge per-token fees, making automated overnight background cron jobs expensive over time. Creates fragility: Closed services suffer outages, policy changes, and sudden price hikes. Open innovation changes the game. By using open-weight models like Qwen 2.5 running locally via Ollama or over self-controlled Cloudflare tunnels, LazyMorning demonstrates that users don't need to sacrifice their privacy or pay monthly API subscriptions to get intelligent, automated life assistance. My Agent Session Built with pair-programming assistance from Antigravity. You can view or replay the session here: The Lazy Payoff Saved 20–30 minutes every morning: Eliminates the cognitive load of opening 5 different tools (Notes app, Todoist, Markdown files, Slack reminders) just to figure out what to do first. Zero Morning Panic: Instead of waking up to an overwhelming wall of 20 unorganized tasks, you get Top 3 Priorities and a gentle Suggested First Step. Effortless Overnight Automation: The in-process APScheduler generates everything before you open your eyes. You literally wake up to finished organization. Prize Categories Slow and Steady Grand Prize Best Use of Open-Weight Models (Qwen 2.5 & Ollama) Best Local-First / Privacy-Preserving AI Application Most Creative / Fun UI & Mascot Design

articles.title: AI Cleanup: How Freelancers Can Earn Without Writing Code
articles.description: Freelancers often feel stuck between wanting more projects and fearing they need to learn programming first. The good news is there are jobs that only require a basic understanding of AI and the ability to run a few tools. This post explains what AI cleanup is, where to find gigs, which skills you need, real-world pricing, and a step-by-step plan to start earning. What Is AI Cleanup? AI cleanup means using artificial-intelligence models to remove noise, duplicates, or labeling errors from data, images, or text. Typical tasks include: Removing unwanted backgrounds from photos. Auto-correcting spelling in user comments. Sorting a mislabeled image dataset. According to Kompas.com, AI cleanup services are in high demand as companies look to speed up their data pipelines. Platforms That List AI Cleanup Projects Upwork – Search under Data Cleaning or Image Annotation. Many clients include the phrase “AI cleanup” in the job description. Fiverr – Create a gig titled something like “Clean your image dataset with AI.” Gigs start at $5 (≈ Rp 75 000) and can be upsold with premium packages. Sribulancer – An Indonesian platform that often posts local-language projects, e.g., “Bersihkan dataset komentar forum.” Freelance.com – Offers short-term projects with clear daily budgets. All of these platforms use escrow to protect payments, which reduces the risk of non-payment. Skills You Need Skill Difficulty How to Learn Basic AI concepts (supervised vs unsupervised) Low Free courses on Coursera or YouTube – search “AI basics for non-programmers.” Using the Cleanformer tool Medium Official docs: https://cleanformer.ai/docs OpenAI API (ChatGPT, DALL·E) for text-to-text cleaning OpenAI’s tutorial pages; a one-line Python example is enough. Result evaluation (accuracy checks, visual inspection) Practice with sample datasets on Kaggle, e.g., Cats vs Dogs You don’t need to write complex code. Many tools provide drag-and-drop interfaces or simple command-line commands. Real-World Project Examples and Pricing 1. Clean an E-Commerce Image Dataset Description: 2,000 product photos with inconsistent backgrounds, some blurry, and many duplicates. Tool: Cleanformer + a tiny Python script for duplicate detection. Time: 12-15 hours. Rate: Rp 800 000 – Rp 1 000 000 (depends on speed). 2. Remove Spam from Blog Comments Description: 5,000 comments, 12 % are spam or ads. Tool: OpenAI Moderation API. Time: 6-8 hours. Rate: Rp 300 000 – Rp 500 000. 3. Fix Typos in Legal Documents Description: 50 PDF files (≈150 pages) with spelling errors and inconsistent formatting. Tool: GPT-4 with a custom prompt for language correction. Time: 10-12 hours. Rate: Rp 400 000 – Rp 600 000. These rates come from several Upwork listings posted over the past three months. Prices can vary based on project complexity and freelancer reputation. Practical Steps to Start an AI Cleanup Project Create a Focused Profile – Add AI Cleanup Specialist to your headline and showcase before-after samples in your portfolio. Pick One Tool to Master – Start with Cleanformer before expanding to other utilities. Take Small Jobs First – Target budgets of Rp 200 000 – Rp 400 000 to build a rating. Use a Proposal Template – Outline the workflow, time estimate, and sample output. Ask for Feedback – Positive reviews boost your chances of higher-paying gigs. Below is a short proposal you can copy-paste: **Subject:** Proposal AI Cleanup for Your Image Dataset Hi [Client Name], I can clean your 2,000 product images by: 1. Removing background noise with Cleanformer. 2. Detecting and deleting duplicate files. 3. Delivering a zip folder with renamed, uniform images. Estimated time: 14 hours. Cost: Rp 850 000 (including revisions). Let me know if you have any questions! Best, [Your Name] Risks and How to Mitigate Them Data Quality: Very noisy datasets may still need manual spot-checks. Always include a quality-check step. API Costs: OpenAI API charges per token. Estimate the cost before quoting a price. Competition: Many freelancers offer similar services. Differentiate yourself with speed, visual quality, or an extra statistical report. Summary AI cleanup = AI-powered data, image, or text cleaning; demand is growing. Main platforms: Upwork, Fiverr, Sribulancer, Freelance.com. Key skills: basic AI theory, Cleanformer, OpenAI API, result evaluation. Typical rates: Rp 200 000 – Rp 1 000 000 per project, depending on volume and complexity. Getting started: craft a niche profile, take small gigs, use a proposal template, and collect reviews. If you want to boost your income without learning to code, AI cleanup is a realistic first step. Follow for daily AI, career, and money-making insights!

articles.title: Is It Drift or Is It the Game? How to Tell Before You Open Your Controller
articles.description: Your character walks left on its own. Your camera slowly pans up. Before you reach for a screwdriver, stop: many of these symptoms are not stick drift at all. A game setting, a deadzone problem, or a second input device can look exactly like a broken stick. Checking in the right order saves you from opening a controller that was never faulty. Start outside the game Drift means the controller itself is sending movement when you are not touching the stick. So test the controller, not the game. Connect it to a PC, open a browser-based tester, and leave both sticks untouched for 30 seconds. You can test your controller online in a couple of minutes, with no download. Watch the stick dot and the axis values. If the dot stays centered and the values stay at zero, the hardware is probably fine. If the dot creeps in one direction, or an axis value sits above zero at rest, you have real drift to investigate. This one step changes the whole repair plan. A centered stick points to software. A creeping stick points to cleaning, recalibration, or a worn sensor. Signs it is probably the game Try these clues before you blame the hardware: The problem happens in only one game, but the same controller is steady in other games and in the tester. Camera movement changes when you change in-game sensitivity, invert settings, or aim assist. The issue stops when you unplug a second controller, a flight stick, or another input device. A game update, a new controller profile, or a Steam Input layout changed the behavior. In these cases, reset the in-game controls to default, check the deadzone setting, and try a different controller profile. On PC, also check whether Steam Input is remapping your sticks in a way the game does not expect. Signs it is probably drift Drift is more likely when: The tester shows movement with your hands off the controller. The same direction creeps in every game and in menus. The stick does not return cleanly to center after you release it. Increasing the deadzone hides the problem, but only for a while, and you need a larger deadzone each week. A deadzone increase is a useful test, not a cure. If a small deadzone hides the movement, the sensor may still be borderline. If you need a very large deadzone to stop the creep, the sensor is likely worn. A simple test order that works Test at rest in a browser tester and note which stick and direction moves. Test in a second game. If only one game is affected, check that game's settings first. Clean around the stick base with compressed air, rotate the stick slowly in full circles, and retest. Recalibrate or reset the controller, check for a firmware update, and retest. Only then decide about repair: a module replacement for a worn sensor, or a repair shop if soldering is involved. When opening the controller makes sense Open it only after the tester confirms drift and after cleaning and recalibration have failed. At that point you are fixing a known sensor problem, not guessing. Keep track of screws, take a photo before you disconnect anything, and do not force a module that does not match your model. If the tester is steady and the problem follows one game, keep the screwdriver in the drawer. Fix the setting, the profile, or the conflicting input device instead. That is the fastest repair of all, because there was nothing to repair in the hardware.

articles.title: Weekend - China warns of countermeasures as US Treasury widens tech investment curbs to biotech
articles.description: The proposal adds to already tense US-China relations and keeps headline risk elevated for Chinese technology and biotech stocks, including US-listed ADRs and the Hang Seng Tech index. Biotech is the sector most directly exposed, since it is the newly targeted industry and has relied more heavily on cross-border funding than areas already under restriction. Beijing has not named the countermeasures it might take, and that vagueness tends to keep investors cautious until the response becomes clear. A long public comment period leaves time for negotiation, but it also stretches the uncertainty out for months, which could weigh on risk appetite toward China-exposed assets and the offshore yuan if rhetoric escalates. -- Washington wants to stop US capital from funding China’s next generation of strategic technology, and Beijing is signalling that it will not take the move quietly. Summary: On Thursday the US Treasury proposed a rule expanding the Outbound Investment Security Program, tightening limits on US investment in hypersonics, quantum, high-performance computing, supercomputing and AI in China, Russia and North Korea The rule also adds biotechnology to the targeted sectors, an addition sought by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent China’s commerce ministry said on Saturday the move discriminatorily widens China-related restrictions, overstretches national security and would damage bilateral economic ties Beijing said it will monitor developments and reserves the right to take unspecified countermeasures The proposal faces a public comment period before a final rule is issued Separately, the State Department this week sanctioned five Chinese companies linked to former Google engineer Linwei Ding, convicted this year of stealing AI trade secrets, drawing further objections from Beijing China has urged the United States to reconsider a proposed rule that would further restrict American investment in its technology sector, warning that the measure would harm trade relations and that Beijing reserves the right to retaliate. China’s commerce ministry voiced firm opposition on Saturday in a statement carried by the state-run Global Times, according to a report by The Hill. A ministry spokesperson said the proposal widens China-related investment restrictions in a discriminatory way and described it as a classic example of stretching the concept of national security too far. The ministry said it would watch subsequent developments closely, warned the rule would damage economic ties between the two countries, and said China retains the right to take corresponding measures, without specifying what those might be. The US Treasury Department unveiled the proposal on Thursday. It would expand existing restrictions under the Outbound Investment Security Program covering hypersonic systems, quantum information technologies, high-performance computing, supercomputing and artificial intelligence. The program aims to stop a small group of countries designated as foreign adversaries, namely China, Russia and North Korea, from using US capital to advance their own technological capabilities. The proposed rule would also bring the biotechnology industry within the program’s scope, an addition that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had pushed for, according to a department press release. Bessent said the changes would strengthen the program and prevent adversaries from using American investment to build critical technologies that threaten US national security. The measure must go through a public comment period before Treasury issues a final version, leaving room for revisions and for further diplomatic exchanges in the meantime. The proposal lands days after the State Department imposed sanctions on five Chinese companies connected to Linwei Ding, a former Google engineer convicted earlier this year of stealing trade secrets related to artificial intelligence. Beijing also objected to those penalties, saying they seriously harm the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese businesses. Taken together, the two moves underline Washington’s widening focus on technology and capital flows as a front in its rivalry with China. Beijing’s eventual response is now the key variable for investors and policymakers alike. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
